areas.name: Diamond Peak
areas.blurb: Diamond Peak is a glacier-carved volcano, less than 100,000 years old, that stands at the center of the Diamond Peak Wilderness south of Willamette Pass, straddling the Cascade crest between Lane and Klamath counties. Its long ridges rise above a lake-dotted forest traversed by the Pacific Crest Trail, and its summit, reached by a non-technical scramble with an exposed final ridge, looks out over the central Oregon Cascades.

areas.name: Three Sisters Traverses
areas.blurb: Multi-peak link-ups across the Three Sisters. They cross several summits, so they are filed here rather than under any one peak.

areas.name: Wallowa Mountains Traverses
areas.blurb: Ridge traverses and multi-peak scrambles in the Wallowa Mountains. They cross several summits, so they are filed here rather than under any one peak.

routes.name: South Side (Hogsback)
routes.rock_grade: Steep snow to about 45° in the Old Chute; glacier travel near the top
routes.best_season: April through June, when a firm, freeze-thawed snowpack covers the upper mountain and the bergschrund is usually still bridged. Later in summer the upper slopes melt out into loose rock and ice, and rockfall and crevasse problems grow.
routes.overview: The most-climbed route on Oregon's highest peak, starting from the lodge on its south flank and following the ski area, then a snow ridge between steaming fumaroles, to the summit ridge. Most of it is a long snow walk, but the last thousand feet is steep, exposed snow above a bergschrund with rockfall and icefall from the surrounding cliffs. It is usually done in one long day with a very early start.
routes.beta: From the top of the ski area, climb the snowfield toward the prominent dark buttress of Crater Rock and pass it on its east (climber's right) side, above the sulfur-smelling fumarole area of Devil's Kitchen, to reach the Hogsback, a narrow snow ridge on the north side of Crater Rock that leads up toward the summit cliffs. Put crampons on at its base. The Hogsback ends below a bergschrund that crosses the slope; how it is passed changes through the season. Above it, the Pearly Gates are a narrow, Y-shaped gully through the rime-coated rock straight ahead; they are the most direct finish but are often icy or melted out. The more common finish now is the Old Chute: from the low point on the Hogsback crest, drop slightly to the north side and climb a broad steep face into a narrowing chute through the summit cliffs, steepening to around 45° before topping out on the summit ridge. Walk the ridge east to the true summit, staying well back from cornices overhanging the north face.
routes.approach: From the parking lot at Timberline Lodge, head north past the lodge to the marked climbers' trail, which follows the east edge of the ski runs. The Silcox Hut is roughly a thousand feet above the start. Keep climbing on the east side of the groomed runs and out of the way of snowcats and skiers, up past the top of the Palmer lift at about 8,500 ft. Above that, continue up the snowfield toward Crater Rock, passing the steaming fumarole area of Devil's Kitchen and the Hot Rocks, and swing around the east side of Crater Rock to the base of the Hogsback.
routes.descent_text: Descend the way you came, most parties reversing the Old Chute facing into the slope, then down the Hogsback and around Crater Rock to the ski area and back to the lodge. In poor visibility, a compass bearing that does not account for the fall line will pull descending parties off to the southwest onto the Zigzag Glacier and toward Mississippi Head, or southeast toward White River Canyon; carry a planned bearing or track and follow it carefully.
routes.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time and be off the steep upper slopes before the sun loosens rime and rock from the cliffs above; many parties aim to summit by mid-morning and turn around by late morning at the latest. Turn back at the Hogsback if the bergschrund crossing looks unsound, the snow is soft and wet, or the upper mountain is in cloud.
routes.bail: Crater Rock and the top of the ski area are the natural retreat points; below the Hogsback the terrain is a long moderate snow slope back to the lodge. Retreating from the Old Chute or Pearly Gates means downclimbing steep snow facing in, so decide before committing to the chute.

pitch_detail.pitch: Timberline Lodge to top of Palmer
pitch_detail.notes: Climbers' trail on the east side of the ski runs, past the Silcox Hut to about 8,500 ft. Watch for snowcats and skiers.
Open snowfield toward the dark buttress of Crater Rock; pass Devil's Kitchen and the Hot Rocks, whose fumaroles give off sulfur gas.

pitch_detail.pitch: Around Crater Rock to the Hogsback
pitch_detail.notes: Pass Crater Rock on its east side and gain the base of the Hogsback. Put crampons on here.
Narrow snow ridge leading up toward the bergschrund below the summit cliffs. Fumarole holes open on either side as the season goes on.
Cross the bergschrund area, then climb the Old Chute to the summit ridge. The Pearly Gates go straight up the narrow gully ahead and are often icy or melted out. Exposed to rockfall and icefall.
Short walk east to the summit. Stay back from cornices over the north face.

gear: Glacier rope and crevasse rescue kit if roping up
what_to_bring: Mt. Hood climbing permit for travel above 9,500 ft
Wilderness permit and climber registration, filled out at the lodge
Oregon Sno-Park permit to park at Timberline from November through April
Warm layers, shell and goggles for wind at the top
Food and water for a 10 to 14 hour day
hazards: Rockfall and icefall from Crater Rock and the Steel Cliff
Bergschrund below the Hogsback
Fumarole holes and toxic gas near Devil's Kitchen and the Hot Rocks
Long sliding falls on hard or icy snow
Avalanche on the upper slopes
Cornices on the summit ridge
Whiteout navigation on descent
obj_haz: Rime and rock released from the cliffs as the sun hits them
Snow bridges over the bergschrund and fumaroles weakening through the day
Sulfur gas pooling in the fumarole areas, enough to suffocate someone who falls into a vent
Crowds on the steep chutes sending down ice and loose snow
routes.watch_out:
Descending in cloud, the fall line pulls parties toward the Zigzag Glacier and Mississippi Head or into White River Canyon
Do not rope together without anchors on the steep chutes; one fall can pull the whole team off
Keep clear of snowcats and ski traffic in the ski area
Afternoon warming turns firm snow to slush and increases rockfall
pro_tips: Go midweek to avoid lines in the chutes
Start between about 1 and 3 AM to be back below Crater Rock before the sun loosens the cliffs
Check the current conditions report; the finish that is in shape changes through the season
Save a track or bearing on the way up for the descent

road.name: Timberline Highway
road.driveNote: Drive to Government Camp on US-26 and take the Timberline Highway up to the lodge parking lots.

routes.rope_note: Many parties climb unroped because a rope team without protection on the steep chutes can turn one slip into a team fall. A rope is useful for the bergschrund crossing and fumarole holes later in the season, and for teams with less experience on glaciers.

access.land_manager: Mt. Hood National Forest (Mount Hood Wilderness above the ski area)
access.parking_pass: Oregon Sno-Park permit, November 1 to April 30
access.permit: Mt. Hood climbing permit (required above 9,500 ft, year-round) plus a free wilderness permit and climber registration at the lodge
access.fees: $20 for 3 days or $50 annual; wilderness permit and registration free

routes.name: South Ridge (from Summit Lake)
routes.rock_grade: Class 2, brief Class 3 moves on the exposed summit ridge
routes.overview: The shortest and most popular way up Diamond Peak: a mellow stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail from Summit Lake, then a steep, cairned climbers' path up the broad south ridge to a false summit. From there a narrow, exposed volcanic spine with a few rock spires leads to the true summit, the only part of the day that needs hands.
routes.beta: Leave the Pacific Crest Trail at a large open, rocky viewpoint marked by cairns and follow the climbers' path straight uphill. It climbs steeply through timber, where large rocks give handholds, then breaks out at treeline onto open ground with views south to Summit Lake, Cowhorn Mountain and Mount Thielsen. Above treeline the path gives way to a steep slope of loose talus and cinder that leads directly to the false summit; trekking poles help here. At the false summit, stow the poles. The true summit lies about 0.4 mi north along the summit ridge, roughly 500 ft higher: the spine looks thin from the false summit but is mostly 3 to 4 ft wide, with a few rock spires that you climb around or over using your hands, and steep drops on both sides. The summit itself is large and flat, with views north to Waldo Lake, the Three Sisters and Mount Bachelor. If the ridge does not feel right, the false summit is a worthwhile objective on its own.
routes.approach: From the Summit Lake trailhead, walk north on the Pacific Crest Trail. This section is gentle, gaining only about 1,000 ft in about 4.5 mi as it winds through forest past several small ponds. At about 3.1 mi, pass a junction with trails to Rockpile and Marie lakes (left) and toward Fawn Lake (right); stay on the PCT. Roughly 1.3 mi farther, where the trail bends at a large open area with rocks and a big view, a cairned climbers' path leaves the trail to the west and heads uphill. This is where you leave the PCT.
routes.descent_text: Reverse the route: back along the summit ridge to the false summit, down the loose talus slope, and down the climbers' path to the PCT, then south to Summit Lake. Below the talus it is easy to keep going straight down the fall line, which puts you out near Marie Lake instead of on the climbers' path; watch for the cairns where the path re-enters the trees, or follow your own recorded track from the ascent.
routes.turnaround: Turn around at the false summit if the ridge is snow-covered or icy, if wind or cloud makes the spine unsafe, or if thunderstorms are building. The false summit is a legitimate stopping point.
routes.bail: Anywhere below the false summit, retreat down the same line to the PCT. There is no safe alternative descent off the summit ridge; go back the way you came.

pitch_detail.notes: About 4.5 mi of gentle forest trail north from Summit Lake, gaining about 1,000 ft past several ponds, to the cairned climbers' path at an open, rocky viewpoint.
Steep, cairned path straight uphill through the trees; large rocks offer handholds in places. Faint in spots, so follow the cairns.

pitch_detail.pitch: Talus slope to the false summit
pitch_detail.notes: Above treeline, a steep slope of loose rock and cinder leads directly to the false summit. Trekking poles help.

pitch_detail.pitch: Summit ridge to the true summit
pitch_detail.notes: About 0.4 mi and roughly 500 ft along a narrow, exposed spine, mostly 3 to 4 ft wide, with a few rock spires that need hands. Put poles away. Steep drops on both sides.

gear: Sturdy boots with good grip on loose rock
Trekking poles (for the talus, stowed for the ridge)
Helmet (optional, useful if other parties are above on the talus)
Ice axe and traction early in the season when snow lingers on the ridge
what_to_bring: Map and a recorded track or GPS for the descent
Plenty of water (little on the upper mountain)
Wind layer and warm layer for the exposed summit ridge
hazards: Exposed, narrow summit ridge with steep drops on both sides
Loose talus and cinder on the steep upper slope
Faint climbers' path that is easy to lose on the way down
Lingering snow and ice on the ridge early in the season
Afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed summit
obj_haz: Rockfall from parties above on the loose upper slope
Lightning on the open ridge
Snow cornices or icy patches on the summit ridge in early season
routes.watch_out:
On the descent, the fall line below the talus leads toward Marie Lake, not back to the climbers' path
The spine looks thinner from the false summit than it is, but the drops are real
The road to Summit Lake is rough and can be slow going
pro_tips: Stow trekking poles at the false summit so both hands are free on the ridge
Late August and September bring fewer mosquitoes and cooler temperatures
Summit Lake has a small first-come, first-served campground, which makes an early start easy
Record your ascent track and follow it down through the trees

road.name: Forest Road 6010 to Summit Lake (via Forest Road 60 from Crescent Lake)
road.status: Rough dirt road; high clearance recommended
road.driveNote: From Highway 58 near Crescent Lake, take Forest Road 60 west, then Forest Road 6010 about 6.5 mi to Summit Lake. Forest Road 6010 is rutted, potholed and rocky, is not maintained for low-clearance cars, and is muddier and harder to drive during early-summer snowmelt. A high-clearance vehicle is strongly recommended. The trailhead can also be reached from the west, from the Oakridge side, via Forest Road 21, where the last stretch to the trailhead is also rough.

timing.recommendedStart: Early morning, to be off the exposed ridge before any afternoon storms

access.land_manager: Deschutes and Willamette National Forests (Diamond Peak Wilderness)
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead, required for day use and overnight trips from June 15 through October 15. Diamond Peak Wilderness is not part of the limited-entry Central Cascades Wilderness permit system. Group size limit is 12.

routes.name: Three Sisters Traverse
routes.rock_grade: Class 4 (loose) on North Sister's summit pinnacle; Class 2-3 on South and Middle Sister
routes.best_season: Mid-July to September, once the trails are clear and the Terrible Traverse on North Sister has melted back or firmed into good steps; before mid-summer that traverse is steep, exposed snow
routes.overview: A long point-to-point link-up of all three Sisters, running south to north from the Devils Lake Trailhead over South Sister, Middle Sister and North Sister and finishing at the Pole Creek Trailhead, so it needs a car shuttle. South and Middle Sister are non-technical scrambles and snow climbs, but North Sister comes last and is the crux: loose Class 3-4 rock, the exposed Terrible Traverse and the rockfall-prone Bowling Alley to its summit pinnacle. Most parties do it as one very long day; some split it with a night between the peaks.
routes.beta: South Sister (10,358'): from the Devils Lake Trailhead, climb the South Sister climbers' trail through forest and onto the open plateau, then continue north up the South Ridge on steep scree, skirting the Lewis Glacier's moraine lake on its west side, to the crater rim and around to the summit - a Class 2 walk-up on loose volcanic rock. Leave the summit down the Northwest Ridge (Class 2, snow early and scree late; the Eugene Glacier snowfield lies along its flank) and drop north toward the saddle with Middle Sister above Camp Lake. Middle Sister (10,047'): climb the South Ridge, mostly big talus (Class 2), to the summit, then descend the North Ridge (Class 2-3; it can hold steep snow or ice early in the season) and follow the upper edge of the Collier Glacier to the saddle between Prouty Point and North Sister. North Sister (10,085'): scramble loose slopes onto the South Ridge and follow climbers' paths that alternate between west-side ledges and the east side at gaps. Below the summit pinnacle, cross the Terrible Traverse - a steep, exposed snowfield with a nasty runout in early and mid-summer, an easy Class 3 scree crossing once melted out - then turn up into the Bowling Alley, a steep, loose gully between the pinnacle's horns. Its headwall is easy but loose Class 4; above it, Class 2-3 leads to the summit block. Reverse the pinnacle and ridge to the Prouty Point saddle to start the exit.
routes.approach: From the Devils Lake Trailhead (5,450') on the Cascade Lakes Highway, cross the highway and follow the South Sister climbers' trail up through forest. After about 1.5 miles it leaves the trees and crosses a trail junction onto the open plateau below South Sister's South Ridge, which leads straight up to the summit.
routes.descent_text: From North Sister, reverse the ridge to the saddle between North Sister and Prouty Point, then descend the lateral moraine on the north side of the Hayden Glacier and follow a climbers' path down beside a creek to the Pole Creek Trail. Cross Soap Creek and follow the trail past the Green Lakes junction and through the old burn - shadeless and dusty by late summer - to the Pole Creek Trailhead (5,300'). From the Prouty Point saddle to the car is roughly 5 miles and 1,600' of descent.
routes.turnaround: Decide at the saddle between Middle and North Sister. If you arrive late, tired or with softening snow on the Terrible Traverse, skip North Sister and descend the Hayden Glacier moraine to Pole Creek - it is the hardest and loosest peak of the day and the one least forgiving of fatigue.
routes.bail: After South Sister, the saddle with Middle Sister drops east to Camp Lake, where the Camp Lake Trail runs about 7 miles north to the Pole Creek Trailhead. After Middle Sister, the Prouty Point saddle leads straight down the Hayden Glacier moraine to the Pole Creek Trail. Either bail ends at the Pole Creek car, so the shuttle still works.
routes.itinerary: Leave a car at the Pole Creek Trailhead and drive the other to the Devils Lake Trailhead. Single day: pre-dawn start up South Sister, down its Northwest Ridge, over Middle Sister south to north, then North Sister, and out to Pole Creek. Two days: camp near Camp Lake or the Hayden Glacier timberline between the peaks (overnight permit required), leaving North Sister for the second morning while the snow is firm.

pitch_detail.notes: South Sister climbers' trail from Devils Lake through forest onto the open plateau.
Steep scree past the Lewis Glacier's moraine lake to the crater rim and around to the summit.
Descend the ridge on snow or scree, then drop toward the saddle with Middle Sister above Camp Lake.
Large talus to the summit.
Descend on snow or scree; steep snow or ice early in the season. Follow the upper edge of the Collier Glacier to the Prouty Point saddle.
Loose slopes onto the ridge; climbers' paths alternate between west-side ledges and the east side at gaps.
Exposed snowfield with a serious runout until it melts out, then loose scree. Many accidents have happened here; many parties rope up and place pickets while it holds snow.
Steep, loose gully between the summit pinnacle's horns; rockfall from other parties is the main danger. Loose Class 4 headwall at the top.
Up and right onto easier ground, then over to the summit block. Descend the same way, rappelling the Bowling Alley if needed.
Back along the ridge to the Prouty Point saddle, down the Hayden Glacier's north lateral moraine and a climbers' path to the Pole Creek Trail, and out to the Pole Creek Trailhead.

what_to_bring: Sun protection - long stretches of open scree, snow and shadeless burn
At least 2 liters of water plus a filter
Navigation for off-trail travel between the peaks
Keys for the shuttle car at Pole Creek
hazards: Rockfall in the Bowling Alley, often knocked down by parties above
Exposed fall on the Terrible Traverse while it holds snow
Loose Class 3-4 volcanic rock throughout North Sister
Steep snow or ice on Middle Sister's North Ridge early in the season
Crevasses where the route skirts the Collier and Hayden glaciers
Fatigue - the technical crux comes last, after two summits
obj_haz: Rockfall
Steep snow with a bad runout
Loose rock
Afternoon thunderstorms
Wind and whiteout on the upper peaks
routes.watch_out:
Do not climb into the Bowling Alley beneath another party
Cross the Terrible Traverse only when the snow will hold a step - hard ice or afternoon slush both raise the stakes
Water is scarce on the peaks late in summer; top up at snowmelt and near Camp Lake
North Sister is reached in the afternoon on this direction - watch the clock and the snow
pro_tips: Set up the shuttle the evening before: Pole Creek and Devils Lake are a long drive apart via Sisters and Bend
Get the Devils Lake day-use permit the moment it releases - that trailhead sells out
Keep pickets and rope accessible but decide on the Terrible Traverse by what you see from the Prouty Point saddle
Bail options from both saddles end at Pole Creek, so the shuttle car covers every exit

road.name: Cascade Lakes Highway (start) and Forest Road 15 (finish)
road.driveNote: Start: from Bend, drive about 29 miles west on the paved Cascade Lakes Highway (46) and turn south at the sign for the Devils Lake Trailhead; the trail starts across the highway. Finish: from Sisters, drive 1.5 miles west on Highway 242, then about 10 miles south on Forest Road 15 to the Pole Creek Trailhead - paved at first, then wide but heavily washboarded gravel. The shuttle between the two runs via Sisters and Bend. Check the Deschutes National Forest for fire closures before driving; the 2026 Akawa Butte Fire closure lies northeast of Sisters, not on either road.

timing.recommendedStart: Before dawn - the traverse is long and North Sister, the crux, comes last

bivy.name: Camp Lake
bivy.notes: Below the saddle between South and Middle Sister. Very windy with limited, popular sites. Camp at least 200' from the shore; no campfires.

bivy.name: Timberline below the Hayden Glacier
bivy.notes: Near the foot of the Hayden Glacier moraine on the exit, about 5 miles above Pole Creek; creeks nearby.

routes.rope_note: A single 60 m rope reaches from rappel anchors near the top of the Bowling Alley. Many parties rope up for the Terrible Traverse while it holds snow; late season, confident parties climb and downclimb North Sister unroped.
rack: 2-4 pickets (when the Terrible Traverse holds snow)
routes.pro_needs: Pickets for the Terrible Traverse while it is snow; slings to back up or replace fixed rappel anchors in the Bowling Alley.

access.land_manager: Deschutes National Forest (Bend-Fort Rock and Sisters Ranger Districts) - Three Sisters Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Yes at both trailheads - Northwest Forest Pass, an interagency pass, or $5 day pass per vehicle
access.permit: Central Cascades Wilderness Permit, June 15 to October 15. Day trips start at Devils Lake, a quota trailhead: reserve a day-use permit for your entry date (released 10 days and 2 days ahead). Overnight trips need a reserved overnight permit for your entry trailhead. Entering at Pole Creek instead, the day-use permit is free and self-issued at the trailhead.
access.fees: Devils Lake day use: $1 per person; overnight: $6 per group; Pole Creek day use: free

routes.name: Hurwal Divide Traverse
routes.best_season: Late July through mid-September, once the snow has melted off the crest and Hurricane Creek has dropped enough to ford
routes.overview: A long, off-trail loop along the high crest of the Wallowas, linking Sacajawea Peak and the Matterhorn to Chief Joseph Mountain by way of the Hurwal Divide and crossing about nine summits over 9,000 feet. Most of it is Class 2 talus and goat-path walking on loose, mixed rock, with short Class 3 scrambling around gendarmes between Sacajawea and the Matterhorn. There is no trail on the crest, no water on the ridge, and the finish is a hard bushwhack back down to Hurricane Creek.
routes.beta: Sacajawea Peak: from the head of Thorp Creek, climb steep fell fields and talus to the ridge and follow it to the summit, the high point of the range, on pale marble and limestone. Sacajawea to the Matterhorn: the crest south carries a handful of gendarmes; stay on the spine for Class 3 moves with moderate exposure, or drop onto the west side in scree to get around them. Expect to pick a line and backtrack at times. The Matterhorn: a broad white limestone summit, easy once you reach it. Back north onto the Hurwal Divide: return toward Sacajawea and turn east along the dog-legged divide, mostly on the right-hand (south/east) side of the crest to avoid exposure, over miles of crumbling shale, talus and scree with goat paths giving occasional relief, to the Hurwal Divide high point. Hurwal Divide to Chief Joseph Mountain: descend about two miles to a saddle, then follow the Chief Joseph ridge north over several intermediate points to the dark basalt summit cap of Chief Joseph Mountain.
routes.approach: From Hurricane Creek Trailhead, walk the Hurricane Creek Trail about 1.8 miles to the unsigned, unmaintained Thorp Creek trail on the right. Ford Hurricane Creek (cold and fast early in the season), cross the wide cobbled wash of Twin Creek without losing the tread, then climb steep switchbacks through burned forest and blowdown to Thorp Creek Meadows below Sacajawea. Fill up on water here: it is the last reliable source until you are back down at Hurricane Creek.
routes.descent_text: From Chief Joseph Mountain there is no trail back to Hurricane Creek. Descend the rocky ridge and then steep forest west toward the creek, through burned regrowth, dense brush, deadfall that collapses underfoot and small cliff bands. Hurricane Creek must then be forded to regain the Hurricane Creek Trail, which leads back down-valley to the trailhead. Allow several hours for the final mile or two; this is often the slowest part of the day.
routes.turnaround: Set a firm time to be on the Matterhorn. If you are not there with enough daylight left for the whole Hurwal Divide, Chief Joseph and a bushwhack descent, go back to Sacajawea and down the Thorp Creek approach you already know instead of pressing on.
routes.bail: The cleanest escape from the Sacajawea–Matterhorn end is back down Thorp Creek to Hurricane Creek. The Matterhorn's standard Class 2 route leads down to Ice Lake, whose trail drops to the West Fork Wallowa River at Wallowa Lake, far from your car. Once you are well along the Hurwal Divide, retreat is slow in either direction; steep scree slopes lead off the divide into Thorp Creek on the west side.
routes.itinerary: Usually done as a very long single day by fast, experienced scramblers, or as a two- or three-night trip with camps at Thorp Creek Meadows and high on the Hurwal Divide. Day trips should start before first light.

pitch_detail.pitch: Hurricane Creek Trail to Thorp Creek Meadows
pitch_detail.notes: Maintained trail, then a ford of Hurricane Creek and an unmaintained, steep, blowdown-choked trail up Thorp Creek. Last water.

pitch_detail.pitch: Thorp Creek Meadows to Sacajawea Peak
pitch_detail.notes: Steep fell fields and talus up to the ridge, then the ridge to the summit.
Gendarmes on the crest; Class 3 with moderate exposure on the spine, or bypass lower on the west side in scree.

pitch_detail.pitch: Matterhorn back along the Hurwal Divide
pitch_detail.notes: Miles of loose shale, talus and scree, mostly just off the crest on the south/east side; goat paths in places. No water.

pitch_detail.pitch: Hurwal Divide to Chief Joseph Mountain
pitch_detail.notes: About two miles down to a saddle, then north along the Chief Joseph ridge over intermediate points to the basalt summit cap.

pitch_detail.pitch: Chief Joseph Mountain to Hurricane Creek Trail
pitch_detail.notes: Trailless descent through steep forest, burned regrowth, deadfall and small cliffs, ending with a ford of Hurricane Creek.

gear: Sturdy boots with good edging for loose rock
Map, compass and GPS with the route loaded
what_to_bring: All the water you will need for the ridge (3–4 L or more)
Long sleeves and pants for the bushwhack
Sandals or a plan for the creek fords
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall
Exposure on the gendarmes between Sacajawea and the Matterhorn
No water on the crest
Cold, fast ford of Hurricane Creek
Afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed ridge
Steep scree
Hard bushwhack through burned forest and deadfall on the descent
obj_haz: Rockfall from loose marble, limestone and shale
Lightning on the crest
Lingering snow patches early in the season
Unstable deadfall and hidden holes in the burn
High, fast water in Hurricane Creek
routes.watch_out:
The Twin Creek wash on the Thorp Creek approach is the easiest place to lose the old trail
Between Sacajawea and the Matterhorn, if a gendarme feels too exposed, back off and go around on the west side
Mountain goats are common on the divide; give them room and do not let them get between you and your line
The descent from Chief Joseph is trailless and cliffy near the creek; allow far more time than the distance suggests
Hurricane Creek may be too deep to ford where you first reach it; look upstream for braided channels
pro_tips: Load water at Thorp Creek Meadows; the ridge is dry
Stay slightly off the crest on the south/east side along the Hurwal Divide to avoid the worst exposure
Scout or research your Chief Joseph descent line in advance; it is the crux of the day for most parties
Start early to be off the high crest before afternoon storms build
Wear long pants and sleeves for the burned-forest bushwhack

road.name: Hurricane Creek Road
road.driveNote: From Enterprise, take River Street 0.4 mile to Hurricane Creek Road and follow it about 8.8 miles; the pavement turns to gravel before the large trailhead parking area. Hurricane Creek Road can also be reached from Joseph.

timing.recommendedStart: Before first light for a single-day attempt

access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass
access.permit: Eagle Cap Wilderness self-issue permit, filled out at the trailhead

routes.name: Krag Peak Traverse
routes.best_season: Late July to September, once snow is off the west-side rib and before autumn storms
routes.overview: A steep, off-trail loop over both summits of Krag Peak, a double-topped peak in the southern Wallowas that rises about 4,500 ft above East Fork Eagle Creek in roughly a mile. You climb a loose rib on the west side to the lower west summit, cross to the higher east summit, follow the crest, and drop to Crater Lake to return by trail. The scrambling is Class 3 on loose rock with some exposure; the trail miles at either end are straightforward.
routes.beta: Walk the East Eagle Trail up the valley for about 1.5 mi, then leave it and head right into the steep basin on Krag Peak's west side. The line climbs the loose, steep rib that divides two prominent drainages; stay on the crest of the rib rather than in the gullies either side. Expect sections of exposure with big loose blocks, and test every hold. The rib tops out on the west (northwest) summit. From there, traverse the crest to the slightly higher east summit, then continue along the ridge crest before descending the rubbly slopes toward Crater Lake. From the lake, pick up the Little Kettle Creek Trail and follow its many switchbacks back down to the East Eagle Trailhead.
routes.approach: From the East Eagle Trailhead, follow the East Eagle Trail (#1910) up the East Fork Eagle Creek valley for about 1.5 mi to where the route leaves the trail and heads right, up the steep basin on Krag Peak's west side.
routes.descent_text: From the east summit, follow the ridge crest and then descend rubbly, loose slopes toward Crater Lake. At the lake, join the Little Kettle Creek Trail (#1945) and follow it down more than 25 switchbacks, through open, sun-exposed slopes that can be overgrown in places, back to the East Eagle Trailhead.
routes.turnaround: Turn around if you have not reached the west summit by early afternoon, if thunderstorms are building, or if the rib is still holding snow or ice.
routes.bail: Before the west summit, the only retreat is reversing the loose rib back to the East Eagle Trail, which is slow and needs care. Once on the summit ridge, the easier way off is to continue east and down the rubbly slopes to Crater Lake and the trail rather than reversing the rib.

pitch_detail.notes: About 1.5 mi up the East Eagle Trail along the valley floor.
Steep, loose rib between two drainages on the west side. Exposure and big loose blocks; the crux of the day.
Cross the crest between the two tops of the double summit; the east summit is the higher.

pitch_detail.pitch: Crest and descent to Crater Lake
pitch_detail.notes: Follow the ridge, then drop rubbly, loose slopes toward Crater Lake.
Little Kettle Creek Trail down many switchbacks to the East Eagle Trailhead.

gear: Sturdy approach shoes or boots with good edging
Map and compass or GPS for the off-trail section
what_to_bring: Plenty of water (the rib and ridge are dry)
Sun protection for the exposed trail descent
Self-issued Wilderness Visitor Permit, filled out at the trailhead
hazards: Loose rock
Exposure
Rockfall
Afternoon thunderstorms
Route finding off-trail
obj_haz: Big loose blocks on the west-side rib
Rockfall from parties above in the drainages
Lightning on the summit ridge
Lingering snow on the rib early in the season
routes.watch_out:
Test every hold on the rib: large blocks can shift
Do not climb directly below another party on loose ground
The descent slopes to Crater Lake are rubbly and ankle-turning
The Little Kettle Creek Trail can be overgrown and rough in places
pro_tips: Stay on the crest of the rib rather than in the loose gullies either side
Start early to be off the ridge before summer afternoon storms
Crater Lake makes a good spot to refill water on the way down if you carry a filter
Leave the smaller East Eagle lot for cars; stock trailers and large rigs fit better at the nearby Little Kettle Creek Trailhead

road.name: Forest Road 77 to Forest Road 7745 (East Eagle Creek)
road.status: Seasonal; not maintained in the off-season
road.driveNote: The trailhead is at the end of FR 7745. From Baker City, take I-84 north about 1 mi to OR-86, follow it about 23 mi to Sparta Road (County Road 852), go 5 mi to County Road 891, and follow it about 5.5 mi as it becomes FR 70. Turn right on FR 7015 for about 5 mi, cross Eagle Creek, turn left on FR 77 for about 2.6 mi, then right on FR 7745 for 6.2 mi to the end. From Richland, follow Eagle Creek Road / FR 7735, FR 7720 and FR 77 to FR 7745. Parking at the East Eagle Trailhead is small; follow current Forest Service directions, as older directions can be wrong after road closures.

timing.recommendedStart: Early morning, to finish the ridge before afternoon thunderstorms

access.permit: Free self-issued Eagle Cap Wilderness Visitor Permit, one per group, at the trailhead
